# 2 Chronicles 3 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview

The Chronicler's account of the temple building is notably brief — 17 verses compared to 46 in 1 Kings 6–7. As Raymond Dillard notes (cited at Precept Austin), the Chronicler assumes the reader knows the Kings account and focuses on details pertinent to the post-exilic community. The chapter moves like a "tour guide" (Geoffrey Kirkland) through the Porch (vv. 3–4), the Holy Place (vv. 5–7), the Most Holy Place (vv. 8–13), the Veil (v. 14), and the Pillars (vv. 15–17).

---

## v. 1 — The Location of the Temple

**Traditional Reading:** The Chronicler uniquely specifies the temple site as "Mount Moriah." This is the only place in the OT where the temple location is so designated (Ellicott). The connection to Genesis 22:2 ("the land of Moriah," where Abraham offered Isaac) is almost universally noted. David Guzik (Enduring Word) writes: "This was the same hill where Abraham offered Isaac, and the same set of hills where Jesus would later die on the cross." John Trapp (quoted by Guzik) adds: "Where Isaac, as a type of Christ, bore the wood, obeyed his father, and should have been sacrificed. Calvary, where our Saviour suffered, was either a part of this mount, or very near unto it."

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary (StudyLight) adds that the site was "consecrated by the offering of Isaac and the gracious appearance of the angel to David." It was "the place selected by David, bought with his money, and prepared by his labours."

Ellicott notes: "There is clearly an allusion to the etymology of MORIAH, which is assumed to signify 'appearance of Jah.' (Comp. Genesis 22:14.)" He translates it as "in the mount of the Appearance of Jah, who appeared unto David his father."

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-3-commentary
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

**Reformed/Baptist View (Desiring God):** John Piper's article on Genesis 22 emphasizes the typological connection: "The same crest of bedrock witnessed (1) Abraham's knife lifted, (2) David's altar stopping the plague, and (3) Solomon's cornerstone laid. Scripture thus stitches one location into three decisive covenant moments." Piper sees Christ "patterned, promised, and present" on Moriah — the son carrying the wood, the substitute sacrifice, and the Angel of the Lord who speaks as God.

**URL:** https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/where-is-jesus-in-the-old-testament

**Pulpit Commentary (disputed identification):** The Pulpit Commentary notes that whether Solomon's Moriah is the same as Abraham's is "more than doubtful." It notes that the Genesis passage speaks of "the land of Moriah" and "one of the mountains" in it, while Solomon's temple site was not a conspicuous height and not a secluded desolate place. The connection to Abraham is "not suggested" in 2 Samuel 24 or 1 Chronicles 21. Nevertheless, the identity theory is "stoutly maintained" by Hengstenberg, Kurtz, Thomson, and Tristram, but opposed by Stanley, Grove, De Wette, and Bleek.

**URL:** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-chronicles-3.html (via Ellicott)

## v. 2 — The Date Construction Began

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon began in "the second day of the second month in the fourth year of his reign" — corresponding to the month of Zif (April–May), about 967 B.C. Guzik notes this was 480 years after the Exodus (1 Kings 6:1), showing how long Israel lived in the Promised Land without a permanent temple. The tabernacle served the nation well for over 400 years.

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew reads "in the second month in the second," with the versions omitting the repetition — "probably a scribe's error." He suggests reading simply "And he began to build in the second month."

Guzik adds: "This doesn't mean that Solomon delayed his obedience for four years. He probably started to organize the work right away. There is some evidence that it took three years to prepare timber from Lebanon."

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/

## v. 3 — The Temple's Foundation Dimensions

**Traditional Reading:** The foundation was 60 cubits long and 20 cubits wide, "according to the old standard" (or "the first measure" — KJV). Gill explains this refers either to the Mosaic tabernacle's cubit or "the pattern David gave to Solomon" (1 Chronicles 28:11), though some understand it as "the greater cubit" (a longer measure). Ellicott notes: "The ancient or Mosaic cubit was one hand-breadth longer than the cubit of later times (Ezekiel 40:5; 43:13)." The Chronicler omits the height (30 cubits, from 1 Kings 6:2). The Pulpit Commentary calculates these as roughly 80 feet by 27 feet (taking the cubit at 1.33 feet).

Ellicott further explains the Hebrew phrasing: "Now these are the things wherein Solomon was instructed" is better rendered "And this is the foundation (or ground-plan) of Solomon." The Hebrew *hûsad* is a hophal infinitive used substantively meaning "to be founded" (as in Ezra 3:11).

**URLs:**
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/3.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## v. 4 — The Portico (Vestibule)

**Traditional Reading:** The portico was 20 cubits long (across the width of the house) and 20 cubits high, overlaid inside with pure gold. Guzik notes that the vestibule was "thirty feet (10 meters) wide and fifteen feet (5 meters) deep, and the same height as the temple proper."

**Textual Issue — the Height:** The Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "one hundred and twenty" cubits for the height, which would make the porch four times the height of the main building (30 cubits). Both Ellicott and Guzik agree this is likely a textual corruption. Ellicott notes: "The Alexandrine MS. of the LXX, and the Arabic version, read 'twenty cubits'; the Syriac omits the whole clause." Modern translations (NIV, REB, NEB) read "twenty cubits high." Ellicott suggests the Hebrew may be a corruption of "and its breadth ten cubits" (compare 1 Kings 6:3).

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## v. 5 — The Main Room (the Holy Place)

**Traditional Reading:** The "greater house" (KJV) or "main room" (BSB) was panelled with cypress ("fir tree" in KJV — actually cypress or juniper), overlaid with fine gold, and decorated with carved palm trees and chains. Gill notes this room was "twice as long as the holy of holies." Ellicott explains: "He covered with planks of fir; or, panelled with fir... The cypress wainscoting was plated with gold." The palm trees and chainwork were carved upon the panels. Ellicott adds that the LXX renders it "carved on it palms and chains," while the Vulgate has "graved on it palms and as it were chainlets intertwining."

The palm tree motif appears also in Ezekiel's temple vision (Ezekiel 41:18) and likely symbolised fruitfulness, beauty, and righteousness (cf. Psalm 92:12).

**URLs:**

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/

## v. 6 — Precious Stones and Gold of Parvaim

**Traditional Reading:** The temple was adorned with precious stones for beauty, and the gold came from Parvaim. This is one of the details unique to Chronicles (not in Kings). Gill devotes extensive discussion to the location of Parvaim: some interpreted it as Peru (dismissed as anachronistic), Bochart suggested Taprobane (Sri Lanka), Kircher suggested Java, Waserus thought it was Parbacia in Havilah (Genesis 2:11), while Pfeiffer "inclines" to identify it with Ophir. Gill concludes Ophir is "as probable as any." The Jewish tradition (Talmud, Yoma 45) held the gold was called Parvaim "because it was red like the blood of parim [oxen]."

Ellicott suggests Parvaim is "perhaps Farwâ, an auriferous region in S. Arabia. Others connect the word with the Sanskrit pûrva, 'eastern,' and seek Parvaim, like Ophir, in India."

The precious stones are not mentioned in the Kings account. Ellicott notes the Vulgate explains the phrase as meaning "a floor of costly marble." Payne (quoted by Guzik) suggests "the reference to 'precious stones' may suggest mosaics, inlaid in the floor."

**URLs:**

- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## v. 7 — Gold Overlay and Carved Cherubim

**Traditional Reading:** Every interior surface — beams, thresholds, walls, and doors — was overlaid with gold, and cherubim were carved on the walls. Guzik connects this to the tabernacle pattern: "when one entered the temple they saw cherubim all around — as one would see in heaven (Psalm 80:1, Isaiah 37:16, and Ezekiel 10:3). These angelic beings worship God perpetually in heaven." He adds: "One might say that we don't worship angels but we do worship with them."

Ellicott notes that 1 Kings 6:29 gives "a fuller account of the mural decorations," and that the cherubim motif was also present in the tabernacle (woven into the inner curtains).

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## v. 8 — The Most Holy Place: Dimensions and Gold

**Traditional Reading:** The Most Holy Place was a perfect cube — 20 cubits long × 20 cubits wide. (1 Kings 6:20 adds the height was also 20 cubits.) It was overlaid with 600 talents of fine gold. Guzik notes this was "a 30-foot (10 meter) cube, completely overlaid with gold."

Ellicott observes that 600 talents is a staggering figure: "Solomon's whole yearly revenue was 666 talents (1 Kings 10:14)." The gold quantity is not given in the Kings account — this is unique to Chronicles.

Guzik, quoting Trapp, draws a Christological application: "Such was Christ's inside (Colossians 2:9); in his outside was no such desirable beauty (Isaiah 53:2); so the Church's glory is inward (Psalm 45:13), in the hidden man of the heart (1 Peter 3:4)." The gold hidden inside the windowless cube illustrates how Christ's true glory and the Church's glory are inward realities.

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## v. 9 — Gold Nails and Upper Chambers

**Traditional Reading:** This verse is unique to Chronicles — nowhere else mentioned except possibly the Vulgate Latin version of 1 Kings 6:21. The nails weighed 50 shekels of gold. Gill notes that "according to the Septuagint and Vulgate Latin versions, each nail weighed so much, which amounted to seventy five pounds of our money." He also cites the pagan writer Eupolemus (via Eusebius), who spoke of these nails as silver, weighing a talent each, "in the form of a woman's breast, and in number four."

Ellicott concurs: "The LXX and Vulg. take this to mean that the weight of each nail was fifty shekels; and this is probably right, for fifty shekels as a total would be a trifling sum to record along with six hundred talents." The nails fastened the golden plates to the wooden wainscoting.

Ellicott also provides important Ancient Near Eastern context: "Nebuchadnezzar, who restored the great temple of Borsippa, says: 'E-zida, the strong house, in the midst thereof I caused to make, with silver, gold, alabaster, bronze... The cedar of the roof of the shrines of Nebo with gold I caused to clothe.'" Similarly, the Assyrian Esarhaddon boasted of making buildings "shine like day with silver and gold." The practice of overlaying temples with precious metals was common among Mesopotamian monarchs.

The "upper area" (BSB) or "upper chambers" (KJV) over the Most Holy Place are mentioned in 1 Chronicles 28:11 (David's plans). These were also overlaid with gold.

**URLs:**
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/3.htm
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## vv. 10–13 — The Two Cherubim in the Most Holy Place

**Traditional Reading:** Inside the Most Holy Place stood two massive sculptured cherubim, overlaid with gold. They were made of oleaster wood (1 Kings 6:23), plated with gold. Each cherub had a wingspan of 10 cubits (two wings of 5 cubits each), so together their wings spanned the entire 20-cubit width of the room — touching the walls on each side and each other in the middle.

Ellicott notes an interesting textual point: "of image work" (KJV "of image work") is literally "a work of statuary" — a Hebrew word occurring only here and "looking suspicious." The LXX renders it "a work of logs," suggesting the original may have been *ma'asēh 'ēçîm*, "woodwork."

Guzik notes they "faced the entrance to this inner room, so as soon as the High Priest entered he saw these giant guardians of the presence of God facing him." Trapp (quoted by Guzik) adds an anti-Catholic polemical note: "If it were image work — cherubims were made like boys — yet this is no plea for Popish images; since they are flatly forbidden; and God made the law for us, not for himself."

Ellicott clarifies their orientation: "The cherubs did not face each other like the cherubim on the mercy seat (Exodus 25:20)." They "stood on their feet, facing the main room" — that is, facing outward toward the Holy Place (and toward the east, since the temple entrance faced east).

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## v. 14 — The Veil

**Traditional Reading:** The veil (Hebrew *pārōkheth*) was made of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, with cherubim woven into it — identical to the tabernacle veil (Exodus 26:31). This curtain separated the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place.

Ellicott notes that the veil "is not mentioned in the existing text of 1 Kings 6:21, which passage, however, speaks of the chains of gold by which the vail was probably suspended."

Guzik develops the Christological significance at length: "Only one man, once a year, could go behind the veil... Spiritually speaking, in dying for our sins Jesus with His own blood entered the Most Holy Place once for all, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12)." He continues: "In the temple, this veil was torn from top to bottom at the death of Jesus (Matthew 27:51), showing that through His death, there is no longer a barrier to the Most Holy place." Selman (quoted by Guzik) poignantly notes: "To most Israelites, therefore, the temple was an unseen world. God had drawn near to them, but the way to him was hedged around with many restrictions."

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

## v. 15 — The Two Pillars: Height

**Traditional Reading:** Solomon made two pillars in front of the temple. The height given here is "thirty-five cubits" combined. However, 1 Kings 7:15 says "eighteen cubits" for each pillar, as do 2 Kings 25:17 and Jeremiah 52:21. Ellicott states that "eighteen" is "no doubt correctly" the original figure. The LXX and Vulgate have "thirty-five," while the Syriac and Arabic have "eighteen."

Guzik notes that 1 Kings 7:15 specifies these pillars were made of bronze (not stone). Each capital (chapiter) on top measured 5 cubits.

The discrepancy between 18 and 35 cubits has been explained in various ways. Some suggest the 35 cubits represents the combined height of both pillars, or includes the capitals, or reflects a scribal transmission issue.

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

---

## v. 16 — Chains and Pomegranates

**Traditional Reading:** Interwoven chains ("wreaths of chainwork") were placed on top of the pillars, and 100 pomegranates were fastened into the chainwork. 

Ellicott notes that the Hebrew "and he made chainwork in the oracle [debîr]" is "clearly corrupt." If one reads *kad-debîr* instead of *bad-debîr* (an "infinitesimal change in Hebrew writing"), the sense becomes "and he made chainwork as in the chancel" — i.e., matching decorations in the Most Holy Place. The LXX transliterated the difficult Hebrew rather than translating it: "He made serserôth in the dabir."

Regarding the pomegranates: 1 Kings 7:20, 42 indicates there were altogether 400 pomegranates — an upper and lower row of 100 each upon the chainwork of each pillar (so 2 Chronicles 4:13). Jeremiah 52:23 agrees with 100.

**URLs:**
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

---

## v. 17 — The Names: Jachin and Boaz

**Traditional Reading:** The pillars were set up in front of the temple, one south and one north. The south pillar was named **Jachin** ("He shall establish") and the north pillar **Boaz** ("In Him is strength" or "In strength").

Guzik draws rich application: "Every time someone came to the house of the LORD in the days of Solomon they said, 'Look! There is "He Shall Establish." And there is "In Him Is Strength."' It set them in the right frame of mind to worship the LORD." He continues: "The house of God was a place where people experienced what the pillars were all about. At that house, people were established in their relationship with God. At that house, people were given strength from the LORD."

The Precept Austin devotionals connect this to the post-exilic audience: "The two pillars, 'Jakin,' meaning 'he establishes,' and 'Boaz,' meaning 'in him is strength,' served as reminders of the covenant (3:17; cf. Deut. 26:18-19; Rev. 3:12)."

**URLs:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/
- https://www.preceptaustin.org/2chronicles_devotionals

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Perspectives

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Emphasises the typological and Christological fulfilment throughout. Strong focus on how the temple prefigures Christ: the gold hidden inside = Christ's inward glory (Colossians 2:9); the torn veil = access to God through Jesus' blood; the pillars = God establishing and strengthening His people. The application consistently moves toward the believer's present access to God: "We are now the temple of God, and the Most Holy Place is open to us through Christ's blood."

**URL:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-3/

### Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper)
Emphasises the sovereignty of God in redemptive history, tracing the "fractal" pattern of Christ through the Old Testament. On Mount Moriah, Piper sees Christ as *patterned* (Isaac carrying the wood), *promised* ("on the mount of the LORD it shall be provided"), and *present* (the Angel of the LORD who speaks as God). The temple site is "the geographic testimony that atonement is God-initiated and blood-dependent."

**URL:** https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/where-is-jesus-in-the-old-testament

### Baptist (Gill's Exposition)
Methodically works through textual and historical details with attention to ancient sources (Eupolemus, Josephus, the Mishnah). Characteristically thorough on weights, measures, and geographical identifications. Takes the "first measure" as likely the pattern David gave Solomon. Devotes extensive discussion to Parvaim's location, surveying multiple theories.

**URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/3.htm

### Anglican (Ellicott's Commentary)
Strong on textual criticism and philology. Notes scribal errors, compares versions (LXX, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic), and provides Ancient Near Eastern context (Nebuchadnezzar's inscriptions, Esarhaddon's building boasts). Careful to distinguish what is unique to Chronicles vs. Kings. Ellicott's approach is restrained on typology but rich on historical and linguistic detail.

**URL:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/3.htm

### Evangelical (Precept Austin)
Synthesises multiple scholarly voices (Dillard, Olley, Boda, Mabie, Konkel, Patterson). Emphasises the Chronicler's purpose for the post-exilic community: the temple story was "not a curious bit of history, but a vital link to their spiritual heritage and identity." Provides extensive discussion of the Temple Mount's continuing significance in redemptive history.

**URL:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-3-commentary

---

## Points of Traditional Disagreement

1. **The identity of Mount Moriah** (v. 1): Whether Solomon's Moriah is the same as Abraham's "land of Moriah" (Genesis 22:2). The Pulpit Commentary presents arguments on both sides. Most evangelical commentators (Guzik, Piper, Trapp) affirm the identification; critical scholars (De Wette, Bleek, Grove) dispute it.

2. **The height of the portico** (v. 4): 120 cubits (MT) vs. 20 cubits (LXX Alexandrinus, modern translations). Most modern commentators and translations regard 120 as a scribal error.

3. **The location of Parvaim** (v. 6): Peru, Sri Lanka, Java, Arabia, India, or Ophir — no consensus exists.

4. **The height of the pillars** (v. 15): 35 cubits combined (Chronicles) vs. 18 cubits each (Kings, Jeremiah). The LXX and Vulgate follow Chronicles; Syriac and Arabic follow Kings.
